speaker: Horace He
title: Horace He: Building Machine Learning Systems for a Trillion Trillion Floating Point Operations
question: Why do distributed machine learning training jobs break the core assumptions of traditional distributed systems?
guest: When getting GPUs to run at scale, distributed ML programs differ fundamentally from traditional distributed systems. Traditional distributed systems are usually trying to scale queries per second: you have many small, interchangeable queries, performance per unit of hardware is not that critical, and you are often willing to double your hardware to get fault tolerance or higher uptime. In ML systems, by contrast, we basically have a single giant query—training your model—with frequent global synchronizations across all of your hardware. Performance is so critical that there is no way we could tolerate a 2x loss in performance for basically any reason. Even in simple data parallelism, where each GPU handles a different slice of the batch, you still have a massive synchronization of parameters after every step because gradients must be synchronized across the entire fleet. And you cannot simply avoid synchronizing parameters to scale easier, because there is a hard mathematical constraint from the ML training side: if you train with too large a batch size, your model simply will not converge properly.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Traditional distributed systems, such as web services and microservices, are built on the assumption that work is divisible into small, independent, stateless units. Any replica can handle any request, failures are isolated, and you recover by retrying or rerouting. Scaling is elastic, and the hardware is cheap, interchangeable, and loosely coupled.

Distributed training violates nearly all of this. A training job is one long-running, tightly coupled, stateful computation: workers must synchronize gradients every step, so they are interdependent rather than independent. One failed or slow node can stall or crash the entire job (stragglers set the pace), and recovery means restarting from a checkpoint rather than retrying a single request. Jobs need gang scheduling, with all workers starting together or not at all, so partial availability is useless. Elastic scaling is hard because changing worker count alters the computation itself, including batch size and data sharding. The hardware is scarce, expensive GPUs connected by high-bandwidth, low-latency interconnects, where topology and placement matter greatly.

In short, training behaves more like a supercomputing (HPC) workload than a cloud service, so fault-tolerance, scheduling, and scaling patterns designed for stateless services don't transfer.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Traditional distributed systems, such as microservice architectures and big-data frameworks, assume loosely coupled tasks, statistical network multiplexing, independent failure domains, and exact deterministic outputs. Distributed machine learning training inverts each of these premises. Instead of processing independent requests or embarrassingly parallel partitions, training workers execute tightly coupled iterations in lockstep, requiring gang scheduling where every accelerator runs simultaneously. Because collective communications like all-reduce synchronize state across barriers at every step, a single straggler or hardware fault stalls the entire job rather than gracefully degrading throughput or allowing isolated task retries. Networking assumptions fail similarly: conventional cloud fabrics rely on oversubscription and packet hashing across millions of uncorrelated small flows, whereas training unleashes periodic, synchronized bursts of massive elephant flows that saturate links and trigger hash collisions. Finally, whereas traditional systems demand bit-exact determinism from largely stateless, disposable workers, ML training maintains massive, continuously mutated model state in accelerator memory while tolerating numerical approximation, lossy compression, and stochasticity.

noweb.answer: Traditional distributed systems assume loosely coupled workers processing independent requests, where individual node failures degrade throughput gracefully and network traffic mixes statistically across many small, unpredictable flows. Distributed machine learning training inverts nearly all of these premises. Training jobs operate as tightly coupled collective computations: hundreds or thousands of accelerators execute lockstep iterations synchronized by global barriers such as all-reduce. Because every worker depends on the others to advance to the next step, a single failed or straggling GPU stalls the entire job rather than allowing healthy nodes to proceed independently, requiring gang scheduling and coordinated checkpoint recovery instead of stateless task retries. On the network, periodic, synchronized gradient exchanges generate massive, simultaneous elephant flows that overwhelm buffers and defeat statistical multiplexing, standard congestion control, and hash-based routing like ECMP. Finally, distributed training upends classic state and consistency trade-offs: workers hold vast, mutable state in accelerator memory rather than statelessly querying external storage, yet the underlying stochastic optimization tolerates numerical approximation and reduced precision where traditional systems demand bit-exact determinism.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Traditional distributed systems are built for many independent, loosely coupled requests. Workers are mostly stateless, failures are partial and isolated, and you add capacity by adding replicas. When a node dies, its requests get retried somewhere else and the rest of the system keeps going.

Large-scale ML training reverses almost all of this. A training job is one huge computation running in lockstep. In every step, thousands of accelerators have to exchange gradients or activations through collective operations like all-reduce. That tight coupling means the slowest GPU, NIC or link sets the pace for the whole cluster. One failed device stalls or crashes the entire job instead of degrading it a little.

The state is also large and lives on the devices: parameters, optimizer state and activations spread across sharded GPUs. You can't just restart a worker cheaply. Recovery depends on expensive checkpoints and on gang-rescheduling the whole job. At this scale hardware faults, including silent data corruption, show up daily, so failure is routine.

Performance is limited by network bandwidth and topology, not by request latency. As a result, where jobs are placed, how links are wired and how well hardware is matched all directly decide throughput.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Traditional distributed systems—like web services, databases, and batch data pipelines—are built around loosely coupled, mostly independent tasks exchanging relatively small messages over commodity networks. They assume partial failures can be isolated by retrying requests, rerouting traffic, or mitigating stragglers through speculative execution, while relying on strict determinism and exact state consistency.

Distributed machine learning training upends these assumptions. Large-scale training runs as a single, tightly coupled synchronous computation across thousands of specialized accelerators. Every few milliseconds, every GPU must participate in massive, high-bandwidth collective operations like AllReduce or AllGather to synchronize gradients and activations. Because progress is lockstep, there is no graceful degradation: a single slow link, thermal throttle, or failed GPU stalls the entire cluster, turning localized faults into global outages that require halting the job and rolling back to a checkpoint. Moreover, training binds huge, rapidly mutating state directly to accelerator memory rather than fungible stateless workers, and its stochastic floating-point math tolerates some numerical approximation yet is uniquely vulnerable to silent hardware corruptions that quietly ruin convergence.

In synchronous training, every worker computes part of the same model update and exchanges results at each step. One slow GPU or congested network link can stall the whole job. A worker failure can force the entire group to restart from a checkpoint and lose progress.

That coupling also changes how resources are scheduled. A training job often needs many GPUs available at the same time and connected by a high-bandwidth network. A cluster can have enough free GPUs on paper and still be unable to run the job efficiently because they’re spread across slow links. The assumptions that workers make independent progress, failures stay local, and machines are interchangeable all become less reliable.

Traditional distributed systems often spread independent requests across machines. If one machine slows down or fails, the system can route work elsewhere while other requests keep moving. Distributed training turns many machines into participants in a single computation. In synchronous training, workers exchange gradients or activations throughout each step, so one slow GPU or congested link can leave the rest waiting.

Failures are harder to isolate, too. Retrying a request is often enough in a serving system, but a training worker holds part of a shared, evolving state. Replacing it requires restoring the right model and optimizer state and rejoining the other workers at a consistent step. Some jobs have to roll back to a checkpoint, losing work across the entire group. As training scales, adding machines increases compute capacity but also increases exposure to stragglers, network bottlenecks, and failures that can stall the whole job.
